Title: Faithful Autoformalization via Roundtrip Verification and Repair
Text:
Faithful Autoformalization via Roundtrip Verification and Repair
Daneshvar Amrollahi†*
Jerry Lopez
Clark Barrett†
†Stanford University, USA
Abstract
When an LLM formalizes natural language,
how do we know the output is faithful? We pro-
pose a roundtrip verification approach which
does not require ground-truth annotations: for-
malize a statement, translate the result back to
natural language, re-formalize, and use a for-
mal tool to check logical equivalence. When
the two formalizations agree, this provides ev-
idence of a faithful formalization. When they
disagree, a diagnosis step identifies which trans-
lation stage failed, and a targeted repair opera-
tor attempts to correct that stage. We evaluate
our approach on 150 traffic rules using Claude
Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.2. Diagnosis-guided re-
pair raises formal equivalence from 45–61%
to 83–85% for both models, outperforming a
random-repair baseline. An independent NLI
analysis confirms that formal equivalence is
correlated with less semantic drift.
1
Introduction
Autoformalization, the translation of natural-
language
statements
into
formal,
machine-
checkable representations, is a rapidly growing
area of NLP research (Wu et al., 2022). Yet a
fundamental question remains largely unaddressed:
when an LLM produces a formalization, how do
we know it faithfully captures the meaning of
the original text?
Existing evaluations rely on
syntactic validity or downstream task success,
neither of which directly tests semantic fidelity.
Furthermore,
when errors are found,
repair
is limited to end-to-end regeneration with no
diagnosis of where meaning was lost (§2).
We propose a framework that addresses both
problems (verification and repair) without requiring
ground-truth formalizations. The key idea is simple
(Figure 1): given a natural-language specification
x, we formalize it (T1), translate the result back
to natural language (T2), and then re-formalize the
*Correspondence: daneshvar@cs.stanford.edu.
result (T3). We call each of these translation steps
a stage. If the pipeline preserves meaning, the
initial and final formalizations should be semanti-
cally equivalent. When they disagree, the point of
divergence localizes the error to a specific stage,
enabling both valuable diagnostic information as
well as the possibility of scoped repair: attempting
to correct only the faulty component rather than re-
generating everything. The framework is agnostic
to the choice of the formalism: it applies whenever
a target formalism admits an equivalence check,
e.g., automated reasoning tools for logical formu-
las, type-checkers for proof assistants, test suites
for code, etc.
We evaluate the framework on 150 traffic rules
from the Texas Transportation Code using two fron-
tier LLMs, Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic) and GPT-
5.2 (OpenAI). For our evaluation, we use a for-
malization based on many-sorted first-order logic,
checking equivalence with an SMT solver (Bar-
rett et al., 2021). We additionally compare our
diagnosis-guided repair against two ablation base-
lines: no repair and repair based on random stage
selection. The results yield two principal findings:
1. Roundtrip analysis helps distinguish faith-
ful from unfaithful formalizations. When
rules do not pass the formal equivalence check,
this provides concrete evidence for and infor-
mation about unfaithful formalization. On
the other hand, rules that do pass the formal
equivalence check exhibit lower semantic drift
compared with those that fail, according to an
independent NLI-based assessment.
2. Diagnosis-guided repair is both more effec-
tive and more efficient than random stage
selection. For both models, diagnosis-guided
repair substantially improves the success rate
of equivalence checking, outperforming repair
with random error-stage selection. Claude’s
full pipeline nearly doubles Random’s repair

Our contributions are:1
(i) We propose a
formalism-agnostic roundtrip verification frame-
work that provides a signal on the truthfulness of
autoformalization without requiring ground-truth
formalizations. (ii) We introduce a stage-level di-
agnosis and scoped repair procedure that localizes
errors to individual translation steps. (iii) We con-
duct a two-model empirical evaluation on 150 rules
showing that diagnosis-guided repair outperforms
random repair, while revealing that diagnosis qual-
ity is model-dependent, a bottleneck that, when
addressed (e.g., via cross-model diagnosis), could
unlock further gains.
2
Related Work
Autoformalization, translating informal natural-
language mathematics into formal,
machine-
checkable representations, has attracted growing
interest since Wu et al. (2022) showed that large
language models can correctly formalize a sig-
nificant portion of competition problems into Is-
abelle/HOL.
Subsequent benchmarks have produced large
NL-formal corpora for proof assistants (Zheng
et al., 2022; Azerbayev et al., 2023; Ying et al.,
2024; Gao et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023a), and
a parallel line uses prover or compiler feedback
to improve autoformalization, e.g., for mapping
informal proofs to formal sketches (Jiang et al.,
2023b), for filtering candidates via Lean 4 diag-
nostics (Lu et al., 2024), for retrieval-augmented
proving (Yang et al., 2023), and for SMT-backed
geometry formalization (Murphy et al., 2024). All
1Code, data, and prompts will be released upon acceptance.
of these efforts either presuppose ground-truth for-
malizations for evaluation or treat compiler accep-
tance as a proxy for correctness. None of them
directly tests whether an autoformalization faith-
fully captures the meaning of the NL input when
no ground-truth formalization exists.
Verification-integrated repair.
Several systems
couple verification with repair: Clover checks mu-
tual consistency among LLM-generated code, doc-
strings, and formal annotations via a Dafny verifier
(Sun et al., 2023), but it assumes the existence of
the formalization from the start. ProofBridge itera-
tively repairs Lean proofs from type-checker feed-
back (Jana et al., 2025). DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5
uses RL with proof-assistant rewards (Xin et al.,
2024). Self-debugging repairs code from execution
results (Chen et al., 2023). These systems treat ver-
ifier feedback as a binary accept/reject signal, but
they do not diagnose which stage of a multi-step
pipeline introduced the error.
Faithfulness without ground truth.
Round-trip
correctness has been used as an evaluation signal in
code generation when checking equivalence via test
suites (Allamanis et al., 2024). In autoformaliza-
tion, recent work uses re-informalization combined
with consistency checks: Li et al. (2024) rank candi-
dates using a mix of symbolic equivalence and em-
bedding similarity over re-informalized text, while
Chen et al. (2026) train a model to self-evaluate
semantic fidelity and iteratively self-correct. These
approaches target mathematics, where the target
formalism provides a natural oracle (a stated the-
orem can be type-checked against its proof). Reg-
ulatory text offers no such oracle, motivating our
use of formal SMT equivalence over the round-trip
artifacts together with stage-level diagnosis and
scoped repair, rather than candidate selection or
single-pass self-correction.
3
Roundtrip Autoformalization
Framework
Target formalism and notation.
Let X denote
the set of natural-language strings. We use Σ to
represent the target formalism. The framework
is agnostic to the specific choice of Σ: all that is
required is for there to be a notion of well-formed
expressions and a notion of formal equivalence. Let
YΣ denote the set of well-formed Σ−expressions.
We write ya ≡Σ yb when two formulas ya, yb ∈YΣ
are equivalent according to Σ. For example, Σ


could be first-order logic with the standard notion
of logical equivalence, or it could be a formalism
based on dependent type theory such as that used by
the Lean 4 theorem prover (de Moura and Ullrich,
2021).
Three translation stages.
We model roundtrip
autoformalization as a composition of three trans-
lation functions:
T1 : X →YΣ
(1)
T2 : YΣ →X
(2)
T3 : X →YΣ
(3)
where T1 performs autoformalization, T2 performs
back-translation, and T3 performs re-formalization.
All three stages operate under the same fixed target
formalism Σ. Each Ti is assumed to be stateless:
successive calls are mutually independent, with
no shared memory or parameter updates between
stages. The framework is agnostic to how each Ti
is realized (e.g., an LLM, a rule-based translator,
or a human annotator). Note that T1 and T3 share
the same type: both translate from natural language
strings to well-formed Σ expressions. We consider
them distinct to maintain generality and also so that
stage-level diagnosis and scoped repair can refer
unambiguously to the pipeline stage at which an
error originates.
Roundtrip instance.
Consider again Figure 1.
Given an input x ∈X, the roundtrip pipeline pro-
duces:
yorig = T1(x) ∈YΣ
(4)
x′ = T2(yorig) ∈X
(5)
yrt = T3(x′) ∈YΣ.
(6)
We refer to yorig as the original formalization and
to yrt as the roundtrip formalization.
Why roundtrip?
The roundtrip construction
yields a verification signal without requiring
ground-truth formalizations. If T1 faithfully cap-
tures the meaning of x, then back-translating and
re-formalizing should recover the same formal se-
mantics. When the two formalizations disagree,
the point of divergence localizes the error.
Formal equivalence.
The primary verification
question is whether yorig ≡Σ yrt.
If not, at
least one translation stage has introduced or lost
meaning, triggering a diagnosis step in which an
LLM judge examines all four pipeline artifacts
(x, yorig, x′, yrt) to identify the responsible stage
and produce a scoped explanation for repair (§4).
Note that if the roundtrip is consistent with the
original (i.e., yorig ≡Σ yrt), correctness is still not
guaranteed: the pipeline may stabilize at a seman-
tically different fixed point where both formaliza-
tions agree yet neither faithfully represents x. We
therefore treat formal consistency as necessary but
not sufficient. In §5, we discuss how to supplement
roundtrip verification with an additional NLI-based
check.
Syntactic well-formedness as prerequisite.
Be-
fore semantic equivalence can be checked, each
formula must be syntactically valid according to
Σ. LLM-generated formulas occasionally violate
grammar or type constraints. We allow up to five
LLM-based correction attempts per formula, which
in our experience suffices to ensure that at least one
parsable encoding is produced.
4
Stage-Based Diagnosis and Iterative
Repair
When yorig ̸≡Σ yrt, the roundtrip instance is for-
mally inconsistent, implying that at least one of the
translation stages introduced semantic drift. How-
ever, the equivalence test alone does not identify
which stage is responsible. We therefore introduce
a stage-based diagnosis and repair procedure that
localizes the failure and applies a targeted repair
operator (Figure 2).
4.1
First-Failure Diagnosis
First-failed stage.
We view the pipeline as an
ordered sequence of stages T1 ≺T2 ≺T3. In-
tuitively, an error introduced earlier may propa-
gate downstream, so we aim to identify the earli-
est stage at which the pipeline ceases to preserve
semantics. Formally specifying natural-language
semantics is beyond the scope of this work. Instead,
diagnosis operates over the observable artifacts
(x, yorig, x′, yrt) and returns an index in {1, 2, 3}.
Diagnosis function.
Let
D : X × YΣ × X × YΣ →{1, 2, 3} × E
(7)
be a diagnosis procedure which, given the roundtrip
artifacts, predicts the first failed stage and produces
an explanation e ∈E, where E is the set of possible
explanations. In our system, D is implemented as
a constrained LLM-based judge and E is simply
X, the set of natural language strings. We enforce


a sequential checking protocol: D must examine
stages strictly in order (first comparing x with yorig
for Stage 1, then yorig with x′ for Stage 2, and
finally x′ with yrt for Stage 3), halting at the first
detected inconsistency.
Scoped diagnostic reasoning.
Critically, the ex-
planation e returned by D is constrained to refer-
ence only the artifacts relevant to the diagnosed
stage. For instance, if Stage 2 is diagnosed as
faulty, the explanation must describe the mismatch
between yorig and x′ without mentioning x or yrt.
This scoping ensures that the diagnostic feedback
can be directly incorporated into the correspond-
ing repair prompt without introducing confounding
information from other pipeline stages.
4.2
Targeted Repair Operators
Repair operators.
A key design principle is that
repairing stage i invalidates all downstream arti-
facts produced by later stages; after repair, we
therefore regenerate all subsequent stages to main-
tain a coherent pipeline state. Each repair operator
receives the relevant artifacts together with the di-
agnostic explanation e produced by D:
R1 : X × YΣ × E →YΣ
(8)
R2 : YΣ × X × E →X
(9)
R3 : X × YΣ × E →YΣ
(10)
where R1 repairs the original formalization, R2
repairs the reconstructed NL, and R3 repairs the
roundtrip formalization. Each Ri is instantiated as
an LLM call operating under the same target for-
malism Σ. The diagnostic explanation e is injected
into the repair prompt, instructing the model to ad-
dress the specific issues identified during diagnosis
rather than regenerating blindly. This feedback-
driven design enables targeted corrections: the re-
pair prompt explicitly states what semantic mis-
match was detected, and the LLM is required to
resolve that mismatch while preserving other as-
pects of the encoding.
4.3
Iterative Repair Loop
Iterative procedure.
We combine verification,
diagnosis, and repair into an iterative loop that at-
tempts to reach formal self-consistency within a
bounded budget. Starting from (x, yorig, x′, yrt),
we repeatedly: (i) check whether yorig ≡Σ yrt,
(ii) if not, diagnose the first-failed stage, apply
the corresponding repair operator, and regenerate

5
Auxiliary Semantic Signal
Bidirectional NLI as a semantic proxy.
We
use natural language inference (NLI) to compare
the original rule x with the reconstructed natural-
language description x′
= T2(yorig).
If the
roundtrip preserves semantics, x and x′ should be
mutually entailing: x entails x′ (nothing lost) and
x′ entails x (nothing spuriously added). We opera-

on MultiNLI (Lewis et al., 2020; Williams et al.,
2018), computing entailment probabilities in both
directions:

Thresholds are conservative. Equivalent demands strong
bidirectional entailment (≥0.7) with near-zero contra-
diction (≤0.2), while Contradiction requires high con-
flict (≥0.6). Because these categories serve as a post-
hoc diagnostic rubric rather than an optimization target,
the exact thresholds affect only the granularity of the
analysis, not the behavior of the system.
Diagnostic categories.
We derive Emin
=
min(E→, E←) for mutual entailment and Cmax =
max(C→, C←) for contradiction. Each rule pair is
classified into one of six categories via the decision
tree in Figure 3 (first match wins). The six cate-
gories (Contradiction, Equivalent, Strengthened,
Weakened, Related, Unrelated) capture not only
whether meaning is preserved but how it drifts, a
distinction that a binary test would obscure.
Diagnostic, not supervisory.
NLI scores are
used only for post-hoc analysis, not as optimiza-
tion targets. The repair loop (§4) operates solely on
formal equivalence. NLI serves as an independent
diagnostic lens, allowing us to ask: when formal
self-consistency is achieved, does semantic fidelity
follow? This separation avoids optimizing for a
noisy proxy while still providing a meaningful sig-
nal. In §7, we cross-tabulate formal equivalence
with NLI categories to reveal where formal consis-
tency diverges from semantic alignment.
6
Experimental Setup
6.1
Domain and Dataset
From law to logic.
We instantiate the framework
on traffic law, a domain that combines natural-
language ambiguity with precise operational re-
quirements (Holzenberger et al., 2020; Blair-Stanek
et al., 2023; Manas et al., 2024). Any statutory do-
main admitting a formal equivalence check could
serve equally well (§3).
Traffic rule corpus.
We evaluate on 150 rules
drawn from the Texas Transportation Code. These
rules govern vehicle behavior on roadways, cov-
ering lane positioning, passing maneuvers, signal-
ing requirements, speed limits, and interactions
with special vehicles (e.g., streetcars, school buses,
emergency vehicles). Each rule is expressed as


a single natural-language sentence or short para-
graph, ranging from simple directives to complex
conditional statements. Each rule passes through
our three-stage translation pipeline, and up to three
repair iterations are appplied, with per-stage diag-
nosis,
6.2
Models and Configuration
Formalism.
A Satisfiability Modulo Theories
(SMT) solver is a tool that can formally deter-
mine whether a set of first-order formulas is satis-
fiable (i.e., whether there exists an interpretation
that makes all of the formulas true) with respect to
some background theory T (Barrett et al., 2010).
An SMT solver returns one of two verdicts: SAT
(a satisfying interpretation exists) or UNSAT (no
such interpretation exists). SMT solvers can check
whether two formulas φ and ψ are logically equiv-
alent (with respect to a theory T), by checking
the satisfiability of ¬(φ = ψ). If the result is
UNSAT, no interpretation can distinguish the two
formulas, certifying equivalence. If SAT, the solver
can return a counterexample demonstrating the dif-
ference. We hand-write a domain schema, a set
of SMT declarations and definitions that provide
a fixed vocabulary for talking about traffic rule
concepts.2 We use the Z3 SMT solver (de Moura
and Bjørner, 2008) to check equivalence, and all
queries resolve in under one second.
Language models and repair.
To assess frame-
work generalizability across model families, we run
the full pipeline with two frontier LLMs: Claude
Opus 4.6 (Anthropic) and GPT-5.2 (OpenAI).
Both use temperature 0.3. Each translation stage
(T1, T2, T3) and repair operator (R1, R2, R3) is
realized as a single stateless LLM call. The do-
main schema is injected into every prompt, and no
context is carried between calls. All stages and op-
erators use the same prompts for both models. The
iterative repair loop (§4) runs for at most K = 3
iterations per rule. This budget balances repair
opportunity against computational cost. Runtime
details are in Appendix D.
NLI model.
For semantic comparison between
original and reconstructed natural language,
we use BART-large fine-tuned on MultiNLI
(facebook/bart-large-mnli). Inference is per-
formed bidirectionally as described in §5.
2The full domain schema is provided in Appendix C.
6.3
Ablation Conditions
To isolate the contribution of diagnosis-guided
stage selection, we compare three approaches:
1. No Repair (Baseline 0):
The roundtrip
pipeline runs without any repair loop. The
initial equivalence check result is final.
2. Random Stage (Baseline 1): The repair loop
runs for up to K=3 iterations, but at each iter-
ation a random stage i ∈{1, 2, 3} is selected
for repair (no diagnosis). The repair operator
still receives the relevant artifacts and regen-
erates downstream stages.
3. Full (Ours): We use the complete pipeline
with diagnosis (§4.1) followed by targeted re-
pair of the diagnosed stage. This is the system
described in Algorithm 1.
All three approaches share the same initial
roundtrip pass (identical yorig, x′, yrt). They differ
only in the repair strategy applied to rules where
the initial equivalence check returns SAT.
7
Results and Analysis
7.1
Roundtrip Equivalence and Repair
Table 1 summarizes the roundtrip pipeline out-
comes for both models. Before any repair, the two
models differ markedly in initial self-consistency:
GPT achieves 92/150 (61.3 %) while Claude starts
at 67/150 (44.7 %), leaving a repair pool of 58
rules for GPT versus 83 for Claude. Diagnosis-
guided repair is effective for both: Claude’s Full
repair approach raises equivalence from 44.7 %
to 85.3 % (+40.6%), and GPT’s from 61.3 % to
82.7 % (+21.4%). Full outperforms Random in
both models. Claude Full achieves 128/150 vs. Ran-
dom’s 100/150 (61 vs. 33 repairs, a near-doubling),
and GPT Full achieves 124/150 vs. Random’s
118/150 (32 vs. 26 repairs). The smaller gap for
GPT reflects its smaller, harder residual pool due
to its higher initial accuracy.
Efficiency.
For Claude, Full achieves 85 % more
repairs than Random with only 8.6 % more LLM
calls, reducing cost-per-repair by 41 % (7.21 vs.
12.27). For GPT, cost-per-repair is higher under
Full (14.56 vs. 9.77) because its T1-concentrated
diagnosis (§7.3) triggers full downstream regener-
ation. Crucially, Full repairs rules that Random
cannot fix at any budget (Claude: 35 exclusive vs.
7; GPT: 15 vs. 9; Figure 5).

7.2
Per-Iteration Repair Progress
Figure 4 shows the cumulative UNSAT count after
each repair iteration for both models. For Claude,
Full repair fixes 34 rules in the first iteration alone,
exceeding Random’s entire three-iteration total of
33. The gap widens at every subsequent iteration.
For GPT, both conditions fix 19 rules in iteration 1,
consistent with the ceiling effect noted above, but
Full pulls ahead in iterations 2–3 (10 + 3 = 13 ad-
ditional) vs. Random (5 + 2 = 7), nearly doubling
the later-iteration yield.
7.3

intensifies in later iterations (41 % at iteration 1, ris-
ing to 71 % at iteration 3). GPT concentrates 83 %
of its selections on T1, with near-zero T2 (3 %).
In both cases, the Random baseline distributes ap-
proximately uniformly (∼33 % each), confirming

Formal vs. Semantic Alignment

Manual inspection of NLI drift flags.
To assess
the reliability of the NLI diagnostic, we manually
inspected a handful of UNSAT rules flagged as
Contradiction or Unrelated across both models (ex-
amples in Appendix F). A minority are NLI false
positives: the original and reconstructed rules are
operationally equivalent, but the NLI model treats
the lexical gap between legal phrasing (e.g., “shall
yield the right-of-way”) and the schema’s oper-
ational vocabulary (“must not enter the intersec-
tion”) as a contradiction (Cmax ≥0.8). The major-
ity exhibit genuine semantic drift, most commonly
negation or exception inversion, where an exemp-
tion (“X does not apply when Y”) is back-translated
as a positive restatement of the obligation. The ad-
justed drift rate is therefore only modestly below
the raw NLI figures, consistent with the lexical-
overlap heuristics documented in adversarial NLI
work (McCoy et al., 2019).
7.5
Residual Failure Analysis
We manually examined the 22 rules that resist re-
pair under Claude Full after three iterations and
identified three failure modes (some rules exhibit
more than one). The dominant mode (∼14 rules) is
schema vocabulary gaps: the diagnosis correctly
identifies a missing semantic distinction, but repair
cannot succeed because the required predicate does
not exist in the domain schema. For example, r095
requires distinguishing “the ends of a safety zone”
from generic proximity, but the schema offers only
a single-argument distance predicate. Rules with
exception clauses (“except momentarily to pick
up or discharge a passenger”) fail similarly when
no predicate captures the exception. The second
mode (∼5 rules) is stage cycling: repairing one
stage introduces or reveals a new error in the next,
producing a 1→2→3 migration across iterations.
These rules involve complex multi-clause condi-
tions where each repair is locally correct but desta-
bilizes a downstream encoding. The third mode
(∼3 rules) is diagnosis fixation: the same stage is
diagnosed in all three iterations, but the repair oper-
ator re-introduces a variant of the same subtle error.
These patterns suggest that increasing the repair
budget alone is unlikely to resolve residual failures.
The primary bottleneck is schema expressiveness
(§8).
8
Conclusion
We presented a formalism-agnostic roundtrip verifi-
cation and repair framework for autoformalization
that requires no ground-truth annotations. Stage-
level diagnosis localizes errors to individual trans-
lation stages, enabling scoped repair rather than
end-to-end regeneration. A two-model ablation
on 150 traffic rules shows that diagnosis-guided
repair outperforms random-stage baselines, reveal-
ing two separable components: the stage-level re-
pair architecture (validated by both models) and
the LLM-based diagnosis (whose quality is model-
dependent). Cross-tabulating solver verdicts with
NLI analysis shows that formally self-consistent
rules exhibit less semantic drift than inconsistent
ones, and since the reconstruction is produced from
the formalization alone, this lends evidence to-
ward faithfulness. However, formal equivalence
alone is not sufficient: a non-trivial fraction of self-
consistent rules still show drift. A residual failure
analysis (§7.5) identifies schema expressiveness
as the primary bottleneck, motivating automated
schema enrichment as a key direction for future
work, alongside scaling to new domains, cross-
model diagnosis, leveraging SMT solver counterex-
amples to improve diagnosis, and integrating se-
mantic checks into the repair loop.


Limitations
Generalizability across domains.
All rules are
drawn from a single statutory source (the Texas
Transportation Code), and it remains an open ques-
tion whether the patterns we observe (diagnosis
concentrating on specific stages, the efficiency ad-
vantage of targeted repair) transfer to structurally
different domains. Moreover, our pipeline treats
each rule as a self-contained unit. Legal and reg-
ulatory texts frequently contain cross-references
between provisions (e.g., “except as provided in
Section 545.062”), and extending the framework to
handle such inter-rule dependencies is a non-trivial
challenge.
Semi-automatic schema design.
A fixed SMT-
LIB schema is necessary because equivalence
checking requires both formalizations to share a
common vocabulary. Our schema was developed in
a semi-automatic process: we manually authored
an initial sketch on a smaller pilot set of rules, then
used an LLM to propose additional sorts, predi-
cates, and enumerated types for the full 150-rule
corpus, and finally refined the result by hand to
eliminate schema smells (e.g., redundant predi-
cates). This effort was substantial and remains a
labor-intensive component of the autoformalization
pipeline. Fully automating schema construction,
for instance by having an LLM iteratively propose
and validate domain predicates, is an important
direction for future work.
Formal equivalence is necessary but not suffi-
cient.
The roundtrip check can detect inequiv-
alence but cannot, on its own, guarantee that a
formalization is faithful. Two formalizations may
be logically equivalent yet both wrong in the same
way, for example if T1 drops a conjunct and T3 re-
produces the same omission. Our NLI cross-check
(§5) provides partial mitigation, but it is an inde-
pendent heuristic, not a formal guarantee.
Risks
Autoformalization outputs generated by this sys-
tem, including those that pass roundtrip verifica-
tion, should not be used in safety-critical appli-
cations, including but not limited to autonomous
systems, medical devices, or safety case documen-
tation, without independent review by a qualified
formal methods expert.
Use of AI Assistants
GitHub Copilot and Claude Code was carefully
used to assist with code implementation, LATEX for-
matting, and paraphrasing during paper writing.
All scientific content, experimental design, analy-
sis, and claims are entirely the authors’ own.

A
Worked Example: Stage 3 Repair
We trace rule r127 from the Claude Opus 4.6
run end-to-end. This rule is initially SAT (non-
equivalent), diagnosed as a Stage 3 (T3) divergence,
and repaired in a single iteration.
Step 1: Original Natural Language
An operator may not drive over an unprotected
fire hose on a street without the consent of the fire
department official in command.
Step 2: Initial Formalization (T1)
(forall ((v Vehicle) (r Roadway) (t Int))
(=> (and (fire_hose_on_roadway r t)
(not (fire_dept_consent v t)))
(not (on_roadway v r t))))
The encoding is a straightforward prohibition: if
a fire hose is present and the operator lacks consent,
the vehicle must not be on that roadway. Stage 1
produces a plausible encoding.
Step 3: Back-translation (T2)
An operator may not drive over a fire hose laid
on a roadway unless the operator has obtained
consent from the fire department.
The reconstructed text faithfully paraphrases the
formula.


Step 4: Re-formalization (T3): the divergence
(forall ((v Vehicle) (r Roadway) (t Int))
(=> (and (on_roadway v r t)
(fire_hose_on_roadway r t)
(not (fire_dept_consent v t)))
(stopped v t)))
The re-formalization changes the consequent:
instead of prohibiting the vehicle from being on the
roadway (not (on_roadway . . . )), it requires
the vehicle to be stopped (stopped v t). These
are semantically different: the original rule says
the operator may not drive over the hose at all, not
that they must merely stop. A stopped vehicle on
the roadway still violates the prohibition.
Step 5: Equivalence Check
The solver checks the satisfiability of ¬(yorig =
yrt) and returns SAT: the two formulas are not
equivalent.
Step 6: Diagnosis
The diagnosis step examines each stage in sequence
and reports:
FIRST FAILED STAGE: 3. The Reconstructed NL
is a prohibition against driving over the fire hose.
This should be encoded such that if a fire hose is
on the roadway and the operator lacks consent,
the operator must not be on that roadway, i.e. the
consequent should be (not (on_roadway v r
t)). However, Phase 3 encodes the consequent
as (stopped v t), meaning the vehicle must be
stopped. A stopped vehicle is not the same as a
vehicle that is not on the roadway. The correct
encoding should prohibit being on the roadway,
rather than requiring a stop.
Step 7: Repair
The repair operator receives the reconstructed NL,
the faulty T3 encoding, and the diagnosis. It pro-
duces a corrected re-formalization that replaces
(stopped v t) with (not (on_roadway v r t)),
restoring the intended prohibition. The post-repair
equivalence check returns UNSAT: the roundtrip
is now self-consistent.

Runtime
Each model–condition pair requires hundreds of
LLM calls: the baseline pipeline alone makes 450
calls (three translations × 150 rules, plus syntax-
correction retries), and each repair condition adds
several hundred more (e.g., 440 for Claude Full).
Across two models and three conditions, the full ex-
periment involves over 2,000 LLM calls. With a 10-
second rate-limit delay between calls, the Claude
baseline pipeline takes roughly 8 hours wall-clock.
The repair phase adds 2–3 hours per condition.
SMT equivalence checks are near-instantaneous
(under 1 second per query). End-to-end cost is
entirely dominated by LLM inference latency and
rate limiting.
Hardware and cost.
All LLM inference was per-
formed via commercial cloud API endpoints (An-
thropic API for Claude Opus 4.6, OpenAI API for
GPT-5.2). No local GPU resources were used. NLI
inference (BART-large-MNLI) and SMT solving
(Z3) were run on a single consumer laptop CPU
(Apple M-series) and completed in under 10 min-
utes for all 150 rules. We report cost in terms of call
counts rather than dollar amounts, as API pricing
varies by model and changes over time.
Environmental impact.
Our workload consists
entirely of inference over a commercial API, with
no model training or fine-tuning.

Abstract: When an LLM formalizes natural language, how do we know the output is faithful? We pro- pose a roundtrip verification approach which does not require ground-truth annotations: for- malize a statement, translate the result back to natural language, re-formalize, and use a for- mal tool to check logical equivalence. When the two formalizations agree, this provides ev- idence of a faithful formalization. When they disagree, a diagnosis step identifies which trans- lation stage failed, and a targeted repair opera- tor attempts to correct that stage. We evaluate our approach on 150 traffic rules using Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.2. Diagnosis-guided re- pair raises formal equivalence from 45–61% to 83–85% for both models, outperforming a random-repair baseline. An independent NLI analysis confirms that formal equivalence is correlated with less semantic drift.
